summary: Defines the NOTIFY message in DNS, which lets a primary server tell its secondary servers right away that a zone has changed. The secondaries can then ask for the update instead of waiting for a timer to expire.

eli5.summary: Rather than checking the mailbox every hour, you get a ring at the door when a package arrives. Everyone finds out about the news quickly.

questions: how do dns slaves learn about zone changes
what is a stealth dns server
does dns notify use udp or tcp
subtitle: How a DNS primary server taps its secondaries on the shoulder the moment a zone changes.

tldr.problem: Secondary DNS servers only learn about zone changes when their refresh timer expires, so long refresh times leave authority servers out of step for a long while after an update.
tldr.mechanism: The master sends a NOTIFY message (DNS opcode 4) for the zone's SOA record to each server in its notify set. A slave that receives it acts as if its refresh timer had just expired and asks its master for the SOA.
tldr.outcome: Changes propagate quickly without shortening refresh times. NOTIFY is a best-effort hint: it never carries data a slave is allowed to trust, and it is checked by an ordinary SOA query.

today: RFC 1996 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1035. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Rationale and Scope
sections.content:
A DNS zone is normally copied from a master server to slave servers by zone transfer. A slave decides when to check for changes using the refresh time in the zone's SOA record. Long refresh times reduce load on masters, but they also mean a changed zone can be out of step across its authority servers for a long interval.

RFC 1996 adds a NOTIFY transaction: an interrupt instead of a poll. The master tells the slaves that the zone has changed, which is hoped to cut propagation delay without unduly increasing the masters' load.

The scope is deliberately narrow. This specification only lets slaves be notified of SOA record changes, though the architecture is meant to be extensible to other record types. It also gives sharper definitions to the roles of master, slave and stealth server, and is described as an addendum to RFC 1035.
sections.eli5: Checking for news on a slow timer is like looking at the mailbox once a day. NOTIFY is a doorbell that rings the moment something new arrives.

sections.title: Server Roles and the Notify Set
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few roles. A slave is an authoritative server that uses zone transfer to get the zone, and every slave is named in the zone's NS records. A master is any authoritative server configured as the source of zone transfer for one or more slaves. The primary master sits at the root of the transfer dependency graph and is named in the SOA MNAME field; by definition there is only one per zone.

A stealth server is like a slave but is not listed in an NS record, so other servers know of it only through static configuration. The notify set is the group of servers to be told about a change. By default it is every server in the NS record set except any server also named in the SOA MNAME, and some implementations let an administrator override it or add servers such as stealth ones.

The servers must form a dependency graph with one primary master. Every other server transfers the zone by AXFR or IXFR from the primary master or from a slave that is also a master, and loops are not permitted.
sections.eli5: One server holds the original copy of a recipe book and others keep photocopies. The notify set is the list of people who get a call when a new page is added.

sections.title: The NOTIFY Message
sections.content:
NOTIFY reuses the standard DNS message format but uses only a subset of its fields. Fields not described are filled with binary zero, and implementations must ignore messages where they are not. Like a QUERY, a NOTIFY request has the QR flag clear and its response has QR set. The response carries no useful information; it only tells the master that the slave got the NOTIFY, so the master can drop the slave from its retry queue.

For the one defined event, an SOA change, the primary master sends a request with opcode NOTIFY (4), response code NOERROR, the AA flag, one question, and the zone name, class and type SOA in the question. The slave's response is identical except that the QR bit is also set, and the query ID must match the request.

A request has QDCOUNT greater than zero. The answer section may carry an unsecure hint of the new record set. A slave may treat a hint that equals its local data as meaning no more work is needed, but the answer section must never be used to update local data, to decide a transfer is needed, or to change refresh timers. This version makes no use of the authority and additional sections, so senders set their counts to 0 and receivers ignore those sections without discarding the whole message.
sections.eli5: The note is just a short card saying which book changed. The person who gets it sends back a copy of the card to say it arrived, and they never just trust what is written on it.

sections.title: How Masters and Slaves Behave
sections.content:
The transport is UDP unless the master has reason to believe TCP is needed, for example because a firewall allows only TCP or because the changed record is too large for a UDP datagram. Over UDP the master repeats the NOTIFY periodically until it gets a matching response, sees an ICMP port-unreachable, or sends too many copies. The response must match on query ID, QNAME, IP source address and UDP source port. The RFC suggests defaults of a 60 second interval and at most 5 retransmissions for UDP, and says additive or exponential backoff is reasonable. With TCP the request is sent once.

A slave ignores a NOTIFY from a host that is not a known master for the zone and logs an error. When it accepts one for QTYPE=SOA, it behaves as though the zone had reached its REFRESH interval: it queries the master that sent the NOTIFY for the SOA, checks whether the SOA SERIAL has increased, and starts a zone transfer (AXFR or IXFR) if so. It queries only the NOTIFY's source, because other masters may not have updated yet. A slave that does not implement NOTIFY replies NOTIMP, and the master then treats the transaction as complete for that slave.

Because a slave only notifies others after it has updated its own copy, a slave in a deep server graph may receive several NOTIFYs for the same change. It should defer a repeat NOTIFY for the same name, class and type until the first transaction finishes, so duplicates do not pummel the master.
sections.eli5: When the doorbell rings, you go ask the person who rang whether the number on the newest page is bigger than the one you have. If it is, you copy the new pages.

sections.title: Details and Examples
sections.content:
Retaining query state across reboots is optional, but it is reasonable to run an SOA NOTIFY transaction for each authority zone when a server starts. Each slave is likely to get several copies of a NOTIFY: one from the primary master and one from each other slave that transfers the zone and then notifies its own peers. Since NOTIFY is sent only after a successful transfer or after finding no update is needed, the last NOTIFY a slave receives is, barring reordering, the one that reflects the latest change.

A master that wants to avoid many simultaneous outbound transfers may delay before notifying each slave, by a random time that must never exceed the SOA REFRESH time. The RFC suggests random delays of between 30 and 60 seconds as adequate for servers sharing a LAN with moderate-sized zones.
sections.eli5: If everyone gets the doorbell at the same instant, they all rush the photocopier. So the owner sometimes waits a random few seconds before ringing each person.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The authors list two security concerns. First, a NOTIFY with a forged IP and UDP source address can make a slave send spurious SOA queries to its masters, which is a benign denial of service if the forged requests are sent very often.

Second, TCP spoofing could be used against a slave given NOTIFY as a way of synchronizing an SOA query, combined with UDP/DNS spoofing to force a zone transfer. Separately, a slave ignores a NOTIFY from a host that is not a known master for the zone, and the answer section of a NOTIFY is never used to update local data.
sections.eli5: Someone could ring your doorbell with a fake name, and you would waste time checking. That is why you only trust the real newest page, never the note itself.
